podcast.body: Oasis wrote this song about a specific hotel, the Columbia Hotel in London (Paddington), which had a reputation as "the Rock and Roll hotel in the UK." They stayed there while recording their first songs and, during their time, "got baked on acid" and threw furniture out the window, some of which landed on the manager's car, leading to their ban from the hotel. "Oasis had plenty of confrontation and hotels around the planet, they wrote at least one song about a hotel."

podcast.body: This track was Oasis's first ever release, appearing as a promo single in 1993, with Noel Gallagher having taken charge of the band's musical direction. It was later included on their debut album, *Definitely Maybe*. "Oasis and Columbia, that was their first ever release, and it would end up on the debut album, definitely maybe."

podcast.body: This was the "famous white label demo" released as a simple 12-inch single with a plain white label by Alan McGee of Creation Records. McGee strategically distributed it to various industry contacts, successfully generating hype that helped propel Oasis towards becoming one of the biggest British bands of the 1990s and, for a time, one of the biggest bands globally. "Here's the famous white label demo of Columbia."

podcast.body: This was the very first single Oasis recorded and the first song Noel Gallagher wrote for the band. It was inspired by an infamous hotel in London, known for its lenient management, where Oasis was eventually banned for life after throwing bar furniture out a window. Musically, it appears to have been inspired by "Swamp Thing" (1986) by The Comelians and "Axe Corner" by Tortuga. It was first performed in early 1992, either January 14th or Valentine's Day, and later featured in their pivotal King Tut's Wawa Hut set on May 31, 1993. A white label demo was released in December 1993, recorded in Real People's studios, and included samples from an unidentified movie, unknown chants, and a BBC interview clip of British politician Tony Benn. This initial release was 100% independent, with music on only one side of a 12-inch vinyl, accompanied by a plain wrapper sticker. Very few copies were pressed, primarily going to journalists and radio DJs. "Columbia was the first Oasis song ever played on the radio. It was featured on a BBC Radio One show called Evening Session."
